newsitem.title: CHILE: German colony says it will not resist Chile police.
newsitem.headline: German colony says it will not resist Chile police.

text.p: Members of a secretive German colony in southern Chile will not put up armed resistance if police raid the settlement looking for its fugitive leader, wanted on child abuse charges, a colony leader said on Sunday.

News reports have said police may move in to Colonia Dignidad (Dignity Colony) to try to arrest Paul Schaeffer, leader of the colony where local authorities charge that Chilean boys were held and sexually abused.
The boys' parents originally sent them to the farm colony in the Andean foothills near the town of Parral, to attend a boarding school.
A colony leader denied the charges and said he did not know the whereabouts of Schaeffer, who is in his early 80s and emigrated to Chile from Germany in the 1960s.

"A whole campaign has been orchestrated against us by some politicians and the news media of such magnitude that it has become true persecution," Hartmutt Hopp, who acts as Schaeffer's spokesman, said on local TV. Asked if colonists would resist a police incursion, he said "absolutely not."

Police said they believed leaders of the colony had some firearms but they do not know how many, nor were they sure Schaeffer was inside. It could take days to search the whole colony, which is surrounded by barbed wire and guarded by burly security men, police said.

Schaeffer issued a statement on Thursday saying he would not surrender because he feared for his life and that he believed Chilean police were framing him. President Eduardo Frei ridiculed that the next day, saying Schaeffer had nothing to fear if he was innocent.

A special prosecutor appointed by Frei's government issued an arrest warrant last year for Schaeffer and later for various other members of the colony, whose several hundred residents speak German and live in spartan conditions, allowing few visitors. The leaders face a battery of charges including kidnapping, child abuse, obstruction of justice and destruction of public property.
Four members who surrended to police last week, two of them German citizens, were released on Saturday on bail -- $250 for each of the Chileans, $2,500 for the two German men.
Police in nearby Talca, about 160 miles (250 km) south of Santiago, reported no unusual movements by security forces near the colony.
